request.system: You are an assistant Game Master.

calls.prompt:
You are auditing a D&D 2024-format monster statblock for MECHANICAL defects.
Deterministic checks (math, DCs, damage bands, known formatting rules) have
already run — do NOT re-check arithmetic, CR calibration, or damage budgets.
Your job is the judgment layer: defects of adjudicability, counterplay, and
internal consistency that pattern-matching cannot catch.

A defect is anything that would cost a GM or a player at the table: an effect
that cannot be adjudicated, a state with no rules-legal response — and equally a
row that is not worth its action, cannot be run in the time a turn allows, or does
not make practical sense for the creature it is on. A row can be perfectly correct
and still be a defect, because a GM who cannot use it got nothing.



WHERE THESE ROWS CAME FROM — this changes what a finding on each is worth:
- OFFICIAL — copied word for word from the published Monster Manual: Actions/Shortbow
- THE BODY'S OWN ROW — ours, from the donor catalog: Actions/Multiattack, Traits/Great Weapon Master
- WRITTEN FOR THIS CREATURE — ours, authored for this sheet: Actions/Greatsword, Traits/Closing Blade

- The OFFICIAL rows are Wizards of the Coast's own text, copied word for word from the published
  Monster Manual with only this sheet's numbers filled in. They are the STANDARD you judge the other
  rows against, and they are NOT under review. Do not flag their wording, their phrasing, their
  RULES, their counterplay, a missing escape DC or duration or limit, how long they take to resolve,
  or whether they are fun. If a published row seems to lack an exit or a cap, that is how the game is
  written — you are not auditing the Monster Manual, and a published row is what a good row looks
  like.
  The ONE thing worth reporting on an official row is a reference to something THIS block does not
  have: its own grapple, or a row it names that no entry here carries. That means OUR assembly broke
  a published row, and it is the most valuable finding you can make.
- THE BODY'S rows are ours, shared with every creature built on this body.
  Judge their soundness as you would any row — but a defect there is fixed once in the catalog, not
  on this sheet, so report it plainly and do not suggest sheet-specific prose for it.
- The rows WRITTEN FOR THIS CREATURE are where a fix will act. Judge them hardest, against all seven
  principles.
Audit against these principles. 1-4 are correctness; 5-7 are whether the block
is any good at a table, and the owner's bar is both:

1. COUNTERPLAY. Every imposed state has a rules-legal path out, written in the
   entry: an escape DC, a repeat save, a fixed duration, a breakable object, or
   an interior-escape clause. This covers conditions (Grappled, Restrained),
   AND any removal from play (swallowed, banished, teleported away, trapped in
   another space). Frequency gates (1/Day, Recharge, "only while Bloodied") do
   NOT count as counterplay — they limit how often, not whether the target has
   agency once affected. An attack-roll-only effect that removes a creature
   from play with no save and no escape is a defect regardless of gating.

2. ADJUDICABILITY. Every effect answers: when does it happen (trigger, timing,
   or action cost), where does it apply (area, range, or target), and when does
   it end (duration or end condition). An aura with no area, a save effect with
   no range, a trait that describes an activity with no action cost, a
   condition with no duration — each is a defect. Also flag any effect whose
   resolution requires information the block does not provide (a referenced
   zone, object, or state that nothing defines or creates — e.g. spores that
   are never applied, a minion that is never created, "its arrival point" with
   no arrival mechanic). An entry with a name but NO rules text at all is
   always a defect.

3. SELF-CONSISTENCY. Entries must not contradict the block or themselves:
   abilities keyed to movement modes the creature lacks, conditions applied to
   targets immune to them by the block's own rider (e.g. Poisoned applied by a
   Poison-immune creature's aura is fine; a rider that only functions against
   Poisoned targets when nothing in the block applies Poisoned is not), riders
   referencing a state no entry creates. The monster referring to itself by a
   name that is not its own is a defect (referent inconsistency). So is an
   entry whose NAME promises a mechanic its text never delivers — a "Steam
   Shroud" that creates no obscurement, a "Reassemble" with no disassembly
   anywhere in the block, a "Spine Shot" that only hides. Swarm or colony
   mechanics (occupying other creatures' spaces, dispersing into components)
   on a creature not typed as a swarm are the same class of defect. So is
   a creature TYPE its content contradicts — a "Giant" that is a bodiless
   planar shade, a "Beast" with innate spellcasting and telepathy — and
   anatomy its components contradict (chitinous claws and insect scuttling
   on a swarm of Tiny Humanoids; a "Fin Slash" on a creature that flies
   but cannot swim; damage types with no shared physical cause on one
   body, like Radiant tendrils plus Poison spore clouds).

4. FORMAT INTEGRITY. Entry text contains only statblock language. Flag any
   design/meta vocabulary ("save-based action", "2024", "condition names",
   "as written", schema or instruction fragments), orphaned sentences detached
   from their entry, stray characters, or UI text. ALSO flag garbled or
   ungrammatical text: doubled words ("the swarm swarm"), broken or
   half-deleted sentences, or subject-verb disagreements. Do NOT report
   capitalization of any kind — not a lowercase word starting a sentence, not a
   capitalized word mid-sentence. A deterministic pass fixes those before ship
   and your findings are capped, so a capitalization report costs a slot a real
   defect needed. Also flag 2014-format save phrasing ("must succeed on a DC X ... saving throw or").

5. TABLE USABILITY. An entry a GM cannot resolve in ~10 seconds mid-combat is
   a defect: nested conditional branches, multi-clause parentheticals defining
   novel procedures, or effects requiring the GM to track state the block gives
   no way to track. Length alone is not the test — a long but linear entry is
   fine; a short entry with three branching conditions is not.

6. WORTH THE ACTION. A row has to be worth choosing on its turn, or worth having
   as a passive. Flag a dead payload — a row named for an element that deals no
   damage of it, a "molten" reaction that deals nothing, a save that imposes a
   condition the target already has. Flag an effect not worth its cost: Prone for
   the movement it costs to stand, a nuisance where the row's own fiction promises
   a threat. Say what it LACKS — the payload, the duration, the teeth — never a
   number and never a comparison to its CR.

7. PRACTICAL SENSE. A row has to be something this creature could plausibly do,
   as written. Flag a mechanic the body cannot perform — tar that pulls a creature
   15 feet, a lunge rendered as a cone, a hoof rider on a creature with claws.
   Flag an effect on terrain or a state that is already so: difficult terrain
   created where the ground is already difficult, a Speed reduction on a target
   that is Restrained and already at Speed 0. Flag a name and a text that describe
   two different abilities.

CALIBRATION — these are NOT defects. Do not flag:
- A pull or push written "straight toward" or "straight away from" the creature in
  a Cone, Line or Emanation. That is the published books' own wording for forced
  movement in an area; the direction is the line between the creature and each target.
- A trait imposing a recurring save WITH timing and area stated (the Stench
  pattern) or triggered on death (Death Burst pattern).
- An attack absent from the Multiattack line — a creature may always use a
  single named attack instead of Multiattack.
- Repeatable single-target hard CC with a save (official precedent: Ghoul,
  Lich). Only flag hard CC (Stunned/Paralyzed/Petrified/Unconscious) that is
  BOTH ungated AND area-targeting AND carries dice damage in the same clause.
- Ally-referencing abilities on an apparently solo monster (known, parked).
- Conditional or qualified resistances, "if available" reuse of Recharge
  actions, additive Multiattack riders.
- A Prone or Grappled condition with no duration: those conditions carry
  their own exit (standing up; the escape DC). Never suggest adding a
  duration to them.
- Anything you suspect is a balance problem. Balance is out of scope — the
  chassis owns it. If your reasoning contains "too strong," "too weak," or a
  comparison to CR, discard the finding.

THE STATBLOCK:
## Unyielded Champion
*Medium Undead, Lawful Evil*

**AC** 14    **Initiative** +3 (13)
**HP** 117 (18d8 + 36)
**Speed** 30 ft.

| Stat | Score | Mod | Save |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| STR | 18 | +4 | +7 |
| DEX | 16 | +3 | +3 |
| CON | 15 | +2 | +5 |
| INT | 6 | -2 | -2 |
| WIS | 8 | -1 | -1 |
| CHA | 5 | -3 | -3 |

**Skills** Athletics +7, Perception +2
**Vulnerabilities** Bludgeoning
**Immunities** Poison; Exhaustion, Poisoned
**Senses** darkvision 60 ft.; Passive Perception 12
**Languages** Understands Common plus one other language but can't speak
**CR** 6 (XP 2,300; PB +3)

### Traits

***Closing Blade.*** While the champion is moving toward a creature it has damaged within the last 24 hours, the champion's Speed can't be reduced and Difficult Terrain doesn't cost it extra movement.

***Great Weapon Master.*** When the champion hits a creature with its Greatsword, the attack deals an extra 3 damage.

### Actions

***Multiattack.*** The champion makes two Greatsword attacks.

***Greatsword.*** *Melee Attack Roll:* +7, reach 5 ft. 21 (5d6 + 4) Slashing damage.

***Shortbow.*** *Ranged Attack Roll:* +6, range 80/320 ft. 16 (3d8 + 3) Piercing damage.

ALSO check the TYPE line ("type_correction"): if the creature's content
plainly contradicts its type — a "Giant" that is a bodiless mist or
planar shade, a "Construct" that is a living spore-bearing fungus — give
the correct type (one of: Aberration, Beast, Celestial, Construct,
Dragon, Elemental, Fey, Fiend, Giant, Humanoid, Monstrosity, Ooze,
Plant, Undead); otherwise null. Correct CLEAR contradictions of
substance, AND types the content never expresses at all — an "Elemental"
whose body and abilities could belong to any animal is a Monstrosity or
Beast. One authentic trait does not outweigh the suite: if MOST of the
abilities express a different type (necrotic magic, Animate Dead, and
life-siphoning on an "Elemental" that merely burrows), correct to the
type the majority expresses. Never retype on theme or mood alone.

ALSO grade the monster's NAME ("name_grade"): A-F on evocativeness, fit
for this creature's type and abilities, and catchiness. A = could sit in
the Monster Manual as-is; B = solid, no reason to change; C = serviceable
but generic or forgettable; D = wrong register or a flat attack
description; F = absurd or misleading. FIT is judged against
what the creature IS — its nature, substance, and story: a psychic
telepath named for swamp muck, or a fire creature named like a frost
spirit, caps at C regardless of how good the name sounds. A name that
is merely a summary of its attack routine also caps at C — names carry
what a creature IS, not what it does. FIT is judged against
what the creature IS — its nature, substance, and story: a psychic
telepath named for swamp muck, or a fire creature named like a frost
spirit, caps at C regardless of how good the name sounds. A name that
is merely a summary of its attack routine also caps at C — names carry
what a creature IS, not what it does. A or B keeps the current
name — C or lower means it will be replaced. Grade the name, not your
ability to invent a different one.

For principle 4 findings ONLY (garbled text, wrong words, grammar,
doubled words, circular phrases), you may ALSO provide a "rewrite": the
minimal replacement for the quoted span that repairs the text. Rules for
rewrites: change as few words as possible; NEVER change any number, DC,
damage type, condition name, or game term; never add or remove mechanics.
The rewrite must BE the replacement text, never a description of the
edit — to delete the span outright, return "" (the empty string) as the
rewrite. A rewrite containing editing language ("replace this sentence
with...") is discarded unapplied.
A rewrite fixes prose, not rules. Findings from other principles never
carry a rewrite.

THE SPAN IS A HANDLE, NOT A CITATION. Quote the PART of the entry that is wrong — the clause, the
phrase, the missing-trigger sentence — because the span is what tells a repair where to work. A span
that is the entry's whole text says only "something here", and a fix handed that returns the same row
reworded. If what is wrong is the entry entire, say so in the issue and quote the one clause that
shows it best.

An entry's NAME can also be the defect. Flag it under principle 3 and
provide a "rename" when the name and the mechanics disagree:
- the name promises a mechanic the text never delivers ("Choir Silence"
  that deafens nobody, a "Reassemble" with no disassembly)
- the name describes the wrong sense or medium for its effect (a "Glare"
  that deafens, a "Breath" that is a thrown rock)
- the name's ADJECTIVE promises an energy the entry never deals (a
  "Burning Claw" dealing only Slashing burns nothing — it is a "Claw"; a
  "Freezing Coil" with no Cold anywhere is a "Coil"). The published books never do
  this: every energy-adjective name in the corpus deals the implied type,
  imposes its condition, or casts a spell that carries it — spell echoes
  are the one exemption
- the name is invented syllables rather than words ("Thul-eg Strike") —
  coined words belong to the creature's own name, never to entries
The rename must be plain English in this creature's register, must
describe what the entry ACTUALLY does, must not duplicate another entry's
name, and must never include a use-limit parenthetical — the engine
appends "(Recharge 5-6)" and "(1/Day)" itself. Never rename Multiattack,
Spellcasting, or Legendary Resistance.

OUTPUT: JSON only, no markdown fences. Report at most 6 findings.
{ "name_grade": "A-F",
  "type_correction": null,
  "element_claims": [],
  "findings": [ { "principle": <1-7>, "section": "<section name>",
  "entry": "<entry name>", "span": "<exact quoted text, verbatim>",
  "issue": "<one sentence>", "suggestion": "<one sentence, direction not prose>",
  "rewrite": "<optional, principle 4 only: the repaired span>",
  "rename": "<optional, name-defect findings only: the replacement entry name>",
  "confidence": "high|medium|low" } ] }
An empty findings array is a correct and common output. Do not manufacture
findings to appear thorough. Every span must be verbatim text from the block —
if you cannot quote it, the finding does not exist.

RESKIN MODE. This block's numbers, DCs, and damage budgets are engine-authored and correct by construction — never flag them. The model-written parts are the entry NAMES, the TRAIT texts, and ONE signature action; your entire value is there:
1. Garbled rules language ("attacks hit the target's AC with advantage" is not adjudicable — supply the rewrite).
2. Semantic contradictions (an Invisible creature targeted by "one creature that can see it"; a sword trait granting immunity to being Blinded).
3. Name-content mismatches (a "Gaze" that throws things; an "of the Fallen" attack dealing plain Piercing — propose a rename).
4. Misspelled entry names ("Withdrawl").
5. Doubled or contradictory limiters ("only once per turn" plus "while active, can't use it again").
6. REDUNDANT RULES — list each benefit the block grants; if a model-written trait duplicates one the chassis already grants (two entries both giving Disadvantage on Opportunity Attacks), or a clause is made dead by another entry (a trait converting damage a row already deals), flag it and supply a rewrite trimming the duplicate clause.
7. STAT-FICTION MISMATCH — a save whose STAT contradicts what the save represents (a Strength save to shake off a scent-lock, a Charisma save to dodge a falling rock). Propose the stat the fiction demands; the DC never changes.
A typical reskin block carries 1-3 such findings; an empty array on a block with model-written traits usually means a MISSED finding, not a clean block — look again before returning empty. The don't-manufacture rule still stands, and every span must be copied character-for-character, capitalization included.

You are REPAIRING one ability of a D&D monster. The sheet below is finished, and one row on it does not work at a table. Rewrite that ONE row into the closed forms below, keeping what makes it interesting. You never write a number: no attack bonus, no damage dice, no DC — the engine prices every row.

THE CREATURE: Unyielded Champion (the champion), CR 6.
THE SHEET AS IT STANDS (every other row stays exactly as it is; never name a row that is not on it):
Actions / Multiattack: The champion makes two Greatsword attacks.
Actions / Greatsword: *Melee Attack Roll:* +7, reach 5 ft. 21 (5d6 + 4) Slashing damage.
Actions / Shortbow: *Ranged Attack Roll:* +6, range 80/320 ft. 16 (3d8 + 3) Piercing damage.
Traits / Closing Blade: While the champion is moving toward a creature it has damaged within the last 24 hours, the champion's Speed can't be reduced and Difficult Terrain doesn't cost it extra movement.
Traits / Great Weapon Master: When the champion hits a creature with its Greatsword, the attack deals an extra 3 damage.

THE ROW TO REPAIR — it is called **"Closing Blade"** and currently reads:
While the champion is moving toward a creature it has damaged within the last 24 hours, the champion's Speed can't be reduced and Difficult Terrain doesn't cost it extra movement.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT:
- The trait requires the GM to track which creatures the champion damaged within the past 24 hours (possibly across a whole prior session), state the block gives no way to track, and it resolves on movement with no defined action or trigger timing. — Tie the benefit to an adjudicable condition visible on the current battlefield, such as a creature currently Bloodied by the champion, rather than a 24-hour history. (about: "While the champion is moving toward a creature it has damaged within the last 24 hours")

WHAT KIND OF DEFECT THAT IS — this decides the shape of the repair, not just its words:
- ADJUDICABILITY. Name the thing the GM cannot find: the trigger and its timing, which check or save is rolled, the direction forced movement goes, where a target lands. Add the missing fact; change nothing else.

KEEP THE NAME "Closing Blade" EXACTLY. Keep the idea — this row exists because it was a nice surprise on this creature, and a GM who likes it should still get it. Change only what makes it unrunnable.

THREE TESTS YOUR REPAIR MUST PASS:
1. SOUND. Everything a GM needs is on the row. No bonus, radius, duration or amount that the GM would have to work out from somewhere else — if a number is needed, use the form's token and let the engine write it.
2. THE ACTION ECONOMY. The row costs something real. A trait that hands out a free attack whenever a condition is met, with no action and no limit, is the defect this test exists to catch — if an effect should fire often, gate it (a recharge, once per turn, or the creature's action).
3. NOT A DEAD ROW. It must be worth choosing on the creature's turn, or worth having as a passive. A row a GM would never pick is as bad as one they cannot run.

IT IS a trait, so the repaired row goes in the "traits" array. Write exactly one row there and leave every other array empty. If the row's SHAPE is itself the defect — a trait that reads like a reaction, an action that should be a passive — answer in the array that shape belongs to instead, and the engine moves the row to where that form lives.

NAMES ALREADY ON THE SHEET — the repaired row keeps "Closing Blade" and must not take any other: "Multiattack", "Greatsword", "Shortbow", "Great Weapon Master".

THE FORMS
- save (a curse, a breath, a shove, a gaze): { "clause", "name", "stat": one of Strength/Dexterity/Constitution/Intelligence/Wisdom/Charisma, "target": "one creature within N feet" | "each creature in a N-foot Cone|Sphere|Line|Emanation", "damage": true|false, "type": one of the damage types or null, "condition": one of the conditions or null, "movement": "pushed up to N feet"|"pulled up to N feet"|null, "success": "half"|"none", "recharge": true|false }.
- trait (a passive, a style, a resource — it costs the creature NOTHING; never write "uses its Reaction" here, that is the reaction form below): { "clause", "name", "trigger": a when/while/if clause or null, "effect": one sentence; write {dc} where a save DC belongs and {dmg} where damage belongs — never a number, "imposes": one of Blinded/Charmed/Deafened/Frightened/Grappled/Paralyzed/Poisoned/Prone/Restrained/Stunned or null, "condition_relation": one of inflicts/requires/immune/self/none, "acts": the name of another creature or object this row makes act, or null, "heals": true if it restores this creature Hit Points every round for free, "mechanics": how many separate things a table must do, "quantities": how many numbers the row promises, "passive_effect": one of ability/bonus/protection/threat/limitation/none }.
- A row that HEALS states the Hit Points as {dmg}, the action it costs, and a limit (a trigger, "1/Day", or "Recharge 5-6"): "restores hit points to the faithful" and "after minutes" are not rows a table can run.
- {dmg} IS DAMAGE AND {dc} IS A SAVE DC. Never write {dmg} where a COUNT belongs — a number of uses, attacks or legendary actions is a plain small integer you write yourself ("can take 3 legendary actions"), because a GM cannot take 4d6 of anything. If a row should be limited, say so with its limit ("1/Day", "Recharge 5-6") and not with a number in the sentence.
- NEVER PROMISE A LIST YOU DO NOT WRITE. "choosing from the options below", "one of the following" and "as listed below" each require the options to follow IN THIS SAME row's text; a row that promises them and stops is a dead row a GM cannot run.
- reaction: { "clause", "name", "trigger": one sentence, "response": one sentence, same tokens, "imposes": one of Blinded/Charmed/Deafened/Frightened/Grappled/Paralyzed/Poisoned/Prone/Restrained/Stunned or null, "condition_relation": one of inflicts/requires/immune/self/none, "acts": the name of another creature or object this row makes act, or null, "heals": true if it restores this creature Hit Points every round for free, "mechanics": how many separate things a table must do, "quantities": how many numbers the row promises }.
- "acts" ON A TRAIT OR REACTION: name anything OTHER than this creature that your row makes act — attack, rise, move, carry, obey — exactly as the sheet above names it, or null. A table can only run it if that thing is a row on the sheet with rules of its own; if it is not, rewrite the row so this creature does the work. (A row that raises "a spore-puppet" needs a spore-puppet on the sheet.)
- "heals" ON A TRAIT OR REACTION: true if the row gives this creature Hit Points back on its own, every round, with no action spent; false otherwise. A one-off heal, a heal that costs an action, and a heal on another creature are all false.
- "quantities" ON A TRAIT OR REACTION: how many separate NUMBERS the row needs a table to know — every damage amount, every distance or area size, every bonus or penalty. Count them and answer the number. Then WRITE every one of them: {dmg} for damage the engine should fill, {dc} for a save DC, and a literal number for a distance or an area ("a 15-foot Emanation", "within 30 feet"). A row that promises a number and does not write it cannot be run at a table and is refused — "gains Temporary Hit Points" with no amount, "an Emanation" with no size, "deals extra Fire damage" with no amount. If the row needs no numbers at all, answer 0. A BONUS YOU ONLY DESCRIBE IS STILL A NUMBER: "deals extra Fire damage", "gains Temporary Hit Points", "is fiercer while Bloodied" each need an amount a table can read, so COUNT them. If you cannot give the amount as {dmg}, do not promise it.
- "mechanics" ON A TRAIT OR REACTION: how many separate things the row makes a table do — count them, and answer the number. One row, one mechanic: a row that turns a blow back AND steps in front of an ally is two, a row that hides it AND heals it is two. Write the one that matters and leave the other out; we take only rows that answer 1.
- "imposes" ON A TRAIT OR REACTION: name the condition the row involves, or null if it involves none. A row that requires one condition and inflicts another names the one it INFLICTS.
- "passive_effect" ON A TRAIT: a trait must change what this creature CAN or CANNOT do. Name which, exactly one of: ability (it can do something other creatures cannot — breathe water, fly past without being struck at, pinpoint metal through stone) | bonus (it rolls better or hits harder under a stated circumstance) | protection (it resists, is immune to, or cannot be given something) | threat (merely standing near it, or striking it, costs the other creature something) | limitation (it CANNOT do something, or pays a price others do not — it can't shape-shift, it must submerge every few hours, it suffers in sunlight) | none. Answer NONE when the row only DESCRIBES the creature — how it waits, watches, perches, stalks, broods or looks. That is prose, not a trait, and we will drop the row: a trait with no positive and no negative effect on the creature is a line a GM cannot run (owner's ruling, 2026-10-30; shipped as the Dayvault Warden's "Patience", which said it "waits motionless on its perch, watching its prey, without taking any action").
- "condition_relation" ON A TRAIT OR REACTION: how the row relates to that condition. Exactly one of: inflicts (the row APPLIES it to a target — the only value that hands the condition out) | requires (the target must ALREADY have it for the row to work: "a creature that has the Prone condition", "a creature it is grappling") | immune (the row says the creature CANNOT be given it) | self (it lands on THIS CREATURE, not a target) | none (no condition involved; answer null for "imposes" too). A word that merely DESCRIBES is not the condition: "a frightening ruin", "a horrifying stench", "a paralysing cold" are prose, not rules — answer none unless the row names the condition as a game effect.
- A clause that is speech goes to "unplaced" with "where": "languages"; pure lore goes to "unplaced" with "where": "description". Never invent a clause the creator did not type. Never write "the unyielded champion" if Unyielded Champion is a person; write "the champion".

THE SAVE'S STAT. Published monsters pair a save with the stat whose faculty the effect attacks, and the same pairings are held to here:
- the row deals damage — Dexterity, or Constitution. Not Strength and not Wisdom, whatever condition rides along with the damage.
- the row's whole effect is moving the target, a shove or a pull or a haul — Strength.
- the row applies a condition and deals no damage — Strength for Prone, Grappled or Restrained; Constitution for Poisoned, Blinded, Deafened, Stunned or Paralyzed; Wisdom for Frightened or Charmed.
- the row does none of those — whichever stat its own fiction asks for.

Answer with ONE JSON object in exactly this shape — the row INSIDE its array. Never a bare row object, and never a key that is not one of these four: "action", "actions", "row" and "ability" are not keys here.
{ "attacks": [], "saves": [ ... ], "traits": [ ... ], "reactions": [ ... ], "crossRef": null, "unplaced": [] }

An answer with every array empty leaves the faulty row on the sheet word for word, which is the worst outcome available here — there is no ready-made row to fall back on. Repair it into one of these forms.

calls.prompt:
You are generating creature intelligence data for a custom D&D 5e statblock.
Analyze the statblock below and produce a JSON object with these fields.

IMPORTANT: Use lowercase field names in the JSON output.

Field: "description" (string, 2 sentences)
Sentence 1: Physical appearance — what players SEE. Be specific and visual.
Sentence 2: Behavioral identity — what this creature IS as a story character.
Use the statblock's abilities, type, and flavor to infer behavior.
If INT is 5 or below, the creature is instinct-driven — say so.
If INT is 6+, describe its personality and approach.

Field: "signature" (string, 1 sentence)
The single most important tactical fact about this creature. What makes
fighting it different from fighting anything else? Lead with the ability
that defines the encounter.

Field: "abilities" (array of strings)
One line per ability from the statblock. Name, brief mechanical summary.
Include actions, reactions, traits, legendary actions, lair actions.
Skip passive senses and basic movement unless unusual.
